"The Round Has Stalled"

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 11 September 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

A stalled round is a process fault or an evidence gap, and the pass reasons tell you which. Read them, fix the gap or pause, then compress what is left into two weeks. Stalls are more common in 2026 than the headline numbers suggest: deals under $100 million took only 12.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of the year, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42%, so many companies are competing for a smaller pool.

This is operating guidance, not investment, legal or financial advice.

What it usually means

A stalled round looks like one thing from the inside. Meetings keep happening and nothing closes. From the outside, it is usually one of five faults.

FaultWhat it looks likeWhere it traces to
Pass reasons never loggedThree firms said no for the same reason in different words; the founder heard three opinionsPipeline tracking
The window drippedOutreach went out as introductions arrived, over months; no fund had to decide while another was decidingWindow compression
Tier 1 went firstThe best-fit funds saw the weakest deck, as practice, and passedList tiering
Diligence waited on the founderHalf-built data room; each homework request took a weekData room readiness
The gap is realNo organic evidence yet; no process fixes thatEvidence

The first four are process. The fifth is evidence. The honest answer to the fifth is to go and get the evidence, then come back.

Why stalls are common in 2026

The headline numbers are records. Crunchbase data summarised by Foley & Lardner shows $159 billion invested globally in the third quarter of 2026, up 53% year on year, with roughly a third going to 27 companies raising rounds of $1 billion or more. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the US in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024.

For a company raising a normal-sized round, the pool is smaller than it looks. Carta's first-half data shows seed capital on its platform falling from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion, and Series B from $13.5 billion to $10.4 billion. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that companies struggling to keep growing quickly faced difficulty raising follow-on rounds. A stall in this market is not proof the company is weak. It is proof that the bar for a normal round moved, and that the process has to work harder to clear it.

Where it traces to

This traces to Run the round like a sales process, with Raise against evidence, not narrative behind it.

The sales-process piece said forty to sixty named funds, warm routes, a three-week window, a pipeline with pass reasons logged. Every process fault above is a step that was skipped or done out of order. The round is not unlucky. It is unmanaged.

The evidence piece said raise on what customers have done. When pass reasons cluster around "too early" or "want to see traction", the round has not stalled. It has arrived at the evidence gap. A good process cannot close a round the evidence has not earned.

The round is not unlucky. It is unmanaged.

The first move this week

Read every pass. Not the summary you wrote at the time, the actual words. Email, call notes, whatever exists. Put each reason on one line in a sheet. Treat each as a closed-lost reason in a sales pipeline: recorded in the buyer's words, then given a category you can count.

Pass reason, in their wordsCountFixable this month?
"Want to see more customer evidence"3Only by selling
"Not our stage"2List fault, remove
"Team gap in go-to-market"1Possibly

If three reasons match, that is the gap. Decide in one sitting whether it can be fixed in weeks or needs months. If weeks, fix it and relaunch. If months, pause the round, tell the live funds why, and name the date you will return. Investors respect a clean pause more than a slow fade.

If no reason repeats, the fault is process. Compress. Take every live conversation and put it inside a two-week window. Tell each fund the date. Overlap creates the urgency the drip never did.

Finish the data room before the window opens. Then hold a rule: every homework answer goes back within 48 hours. Diligence should never wait on you.

The same discipline runs a win-loss programme in sales: the value is in the pattern across losses, which only appears once each loss is written down the same way.

What not to do

Do not widen the list to 400 names. More of the wrong funds produces more passes, not more offers. The list was sized for a reason.

Do not drop the price in a panic. If the gap is evidence, a lower price does not supply it. If the gap is process, the price was never the issue. The market data points the same way: Carta recorded down rounds at 11.4% of rounds in the first quarter of 2026, the lowest in nearly four years and half the 22.2% of early 2024, and PitchBook data put flat and down rounds at 13.1% of US deals in the first half. A cut price is now the exception, and it signals distress more loudly than it did in 2023.

The exception is a company still carrying a 2021 valuation. PitchBook data reported in August 2026 showed companies that last raised in 2021 trading at a median 59.1% discount on secondary markets. For those companies the price may genuinely be the gap, and the pass reasons will usually say so.

Do not keep "ongoing" conversations alive for months. Ask each one for a decision date. A fund that will not give one has passed and is being polite.

How you know it worked

Two signs. Every live fund has a stated decision date inside the next fourteen days. And the pass reason that clustered has stopped appearing in new conversations, because you fixed it or stopped pitching the funds who care about it.

If the round pauses instead, the clock matters. Carta's median gap between seed and Series A is two years. A pause of three months to get evidence is affordable inside that; a slow fade of six months is not.

lowob takeaways

  • Diagnose before you act. Four of the five usual faults are process; one is evidence.
  • Read every pass in the investor's own words. Three matching reasons are the gap.
  • Pause cleanly or compress. A named return date, or a two-week window with stated decision dates.
  • Do not widen the list or cut the price in a panic. Neither fixes an evidence gap.

Common questions

What should I do when my fundraising round stalls?

Log every pass reason in the investor's own words. If reasons cluster, fix the gap or pause with a named return date; if not, compress live conversations into a two-week window with stated decision dates.

Should I lower my valuation if my round has stalled?

Usually not. If the gap is evidence, a lower price does not supply it. If the gap is process, the price was never the issue. The exception is a company still priced at a 2021 valuation, where pass reasons often name the price directly.

How do I create urgency with investors?

Put every live conversation inside one two-week window and tell each fund the date. Overlap creates urgency that a drip of meetings never does.

Why is it hard to raise a normal-sized round in 2026?

Capital is concentrated. Deals under $100 million took 12.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of 2026, down from 43.8% in 2024, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42% year on year.
